title: Shortcrust pastry by hand
subtitle: The rubbing-in method, cold butter, quick hands, rest before rolling
excerpt: Shortcrust pastry is flour and fat rubbed together to a breadcrumb texture, then brought together with cold water. The job is to keep everything cold and stop the moment the dough holds. Overworking develops gluten and makes the pastry tough. The dough needs at least 30 minutes in the fridge before rolling.
sourceNotes: Shortcrust pastry method documented in Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. The 2:1 flour-to-fat ratio has remained the standard for British shortcrust. Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), also covers the rubbing-in method.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough for one 23 cm tart case or top-and-bottom for a 20 cm pie
recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap the disc tightly in cling film and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge before rolling.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch cleanly. Divide into two discs and freeze one for later.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate. The pastry improves with a longer rest.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven (for blind baking); fan oven 170°C

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of breaking cold butter into flour by pressing it between the fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. The aim is to coat flour particles in fat without melting the butter.

A type of pastry where the fat is rubbed into the flour before water is added. The high fat-to-flour ratio shortens the gluten strands, giving the pastry a crumbly, tender texture rather than a chewy one.

content.text: Shortcrust is the standard British pastry for tarts, pies, and quiches. Flour and cold butter are rubbed to breadcrumbs, then cold water binds the dough just enough to roll. Keep everything cold and handle the dough as little as possible.
200 g plain flour to 100 g cold butter, plus a pinch of salt. This 2:1 ratio makes enough pastry for a 23 cm tart. For a pie with a top and bottom, use 300 g flour to 150 g butter.
Cut the cold butter into small cubes and add to the flour. Using your fingertips (not your palms),
rub the butter into the flour

. Press and crumble, lifting the mixture as you work to keep it cool and aerated. Stop when the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs with a few pea-sized lumps of butter still visible. Those lumps create flakiness in the finished pastry.

Sprinkle 3 to 4 tablespoons of cold water over the crumbs, adding it a spoonful at a time. Use a palette knife or butter knife to bring the dough together, cutting through the mixture rather than stirring. As soon as it starts to clump, stop adding water and press the dough into a disc with your hands. It should hold together without being wet or sticky.
Wrap the disc in cling film and chill for at least 30 minutes. The rest relaxes the gluten and firms the butter. Cold
rolls more cleanly and holds its shape better in the tin than dough used straight from the bowl.

attrs.title: If the pastry cracks when rolling

content.text: Cracking means the dough is too cold or too dry. Leave it to sit at room temperature for 5 minutes, then press the cracks together and re-roll. Do not add more water; press the edges together instead.
